---
title: "Array"
description: "From numbered lockers to java.util.ArrayList: contiguous memory, address arithmetic, O(1) indexing versus O(n) insertion, 1.5x growth and amortised copying, one-pass compaction, the array as its own lookup table, and hard interview problems solved math-first."
---

An array keeps its values side by side in one block of memory. That one decision makes reading any position a single sum, and makes inserting in the middle expensive. This lesson counts both costs exactly, opens `java.util.ArrayList` to see how Java grows an array, and then uses the array's indices as a free lookup table to solve hard interview problems.

All code is in [`ArrayLab.java`](ArrayLab.java). Run it from this folder with `java ArrayLab.java`; it checks every number on this page and prints `OK`.

## The problem

A teacher records six test scores in seat order: `[72, 85, 90, 64, 78, 95]`. She wants to:

- read the score in seat 4 **instantly**;
- squeeze a late student's score, 80, into seat 2 without losing the order;
- keep adding scores all year without deciding the class size in advance.

If the scores were written on a chain of notes, each saying where the next note is, then reading seat 4 means walking past four notes first, and seat 1,000,000 means walking a million. An array answers "where is seat $i$?" with one multiplication and one addition. The price is paid elsewhere: to open seat 2, everybody from seat 2 onwards must shuffle along by one.

## Explain it like I'm ten

::: {.callout-tip}
Picture a corridor of identical lockers, each exactly 2 metres wide, starting 100 metres from the door. Locker 0 is at 100 m, locker 1 at 102 m, locker 3 at $100 + 3 \times 2 = 106$ m. You never walk along counting lockers; you work out the distance and go straight there. That is an array: equal-sized boxes in a row, found by arithmetic.

Now a new child needs locker 2, and every locker is full. The only way is for the children in lockers 2, 3, 4 and onwards to each move their things one locker to the right. The more children after locker 2, the longer it takes.

Aditya Bhargava's *Grokking Algorithms* (chapter 2) tells the same story with friends at the cinema: a group that wants to sit **together** needs a row of free seats side by side. When one more friend arrives and the next seat is taken, the whole group has to get up and move to a bigger empty row. That move is exactly what `ArrayList` does when it grows.
:::

## From simple to advanced

### Level 1: one block of memory, found by arithmetic

An array of $n$ elements, each $s$ bytes wide, occupies $n \cdot s$ consecutive bytes. The address of element $i$ is

$$
\operatorname{addr}(i) = b + i \cdot s, \qquad 0 \le i \le n - 1
$$

where:

- $b$ is the base address, where element 0 starts;
- $i$ is the index, counted from 0;
- $s$ is the size of one element in bytes: 4 for an `int`, 8 for a `long` or `double`;
- $n$ is the number of elements, so the valid indices are $0$ to $n - 1$.

Example: an `int` array starting at byte $b = 1000$. Element 3 is at $1000 + 3 \times 4 = 1012$. For a `long` array at the same base it is $1000 + 3 \times 8 = 1024$. Element 0 is at $1000 + 0 \times 4 = 1000$, the base itself, which is why indices start at 0: the index is the distance from the start, measured in elements.

```java
static long address(long base, int index, int elementSize) {
    return base + (long) index * elementSize;
}
```

Java never shows you real addresses, but the JVM does exactly this sum (plus a small fixed header offset) every time you write `a[i]`. It also checks $0 \le i < n$ first and throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` otherwise, which is why a Java array can never read a neighbour's memory by accident. One multiplication and one addition cost the same for $i = 3$ as for $i = 3{,}000{,}000$, so indexing is $O(1)$.

### Level 2: inserting and deleting means shifting

The block has no gaps. To insert at index $k$ in an array holding $n$ elements, every element from $k$ to $n - 1$ moves one place right:

$$
\text{shifts}_{\text{insert}}(k) = n - k, \qquad \text{shifts}_{\text{delete}}(k) = n - 1 - k
$$

where:

- $n$ is the number of elements before the operation;
- $k$ is the index where the new element goes, or the index of the element removed;
- a "shift" is one element copied to its neighbour's place.

Example: the scores `[72, 85, 90, 64, 78, 95]` have $n = 6$. Inserting 80 at $k = 2$ moves 95, 78, 64 and 90: $6 - 2 = 4$ shifts, giving `[72, 85, 80, 90, 64, 78, 95]`. Deleting index 2 again from these 7 elements moves $7 - 1 - 2 = 4$ elements back left.

```java
static int insertAt(int[] a, int size, int index, int value) {
    int shifts = 0;
    for (int i = size; i > index; i--) {   // right to left, so nothing is overwritten
        a[i] = a[i - 1];
        shifts++;
    }
    a[index] = value;
    return shifts;
}
```

The loop runs **right to left**. Going left to right would copy `a[2]` into `a[3]` and then copy that same value into `a[4]`, smearing one score over the whole tail. The lab's `removeAt` is the mirror image and runs left to right.

If every insertion position $k = 0, 1, \dots, n$ is equally likely, the average cost is

$$
\overline{\text{shifts}} = \frac{1}{n + 1} \sum_{k=0}^{n} (n - k) = \frac{1}{n + 1} \cdot \frac{n(n+1)}{2} = \frac{n}{2}
$$

where:

- $\overline{\text{shifts}}$ is the average number of shifts per insertion;
- the sum adds the cost $n - k$ over all $n + 1$ possible positions;
- $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ is the sum $0 + 1 + \dots + n$.

Example: for $n = 6$ the costs at $k = 0, \dots, 6$ are $6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0$. They add up to $21 = \frac{6 \times 7}{2}$, and $21 / 7 = 3 = 6 / 2$. Half the array moves on average, so insertion is $O(n)$. Only appending at the end ($k = n$) is free.

### Level 3: a growable array, as in `java.util.ArrayList`

A plain Java array has a fixed length. `ArrayList` hides a larger array, its **capacity**, and remembers how many slots are really used, its **size**. When the array is full, it allocates a bigger one and copies everything across. The JDK source (`ArrayList.grow`, via `ArraysSupport.newLength`) chooses

$$
c_{\text{new}} = c + \left\lfloor \frac{c}{2} \right\rfloor, \qquad c_0 = 10
$$

where:

- $c$ is the current capacity, the length of the hidden array;
- $\lfloor c/2 \rfloor$ is half of it, rounded down (Java's `c >> 1`);
- $c_0 = 10$ is `DEFAULT_CAPACITY`, allocated by the first `add` to a `new ArrayList<>()`.

Example: $10 \to 10 + 5 = 15 \to 15 + 7 = 22 \to 22 + 11 = 33 \to 33 + 16 = 49 \to 49 + 24 = 73$. Each step multiplies the capacity by about 1.5.

```java
static final class IntList {
    int[] items = new int[10];
    int size;
    int copies;                            // elements copied by all resizes so far

    void add(int value) {
        if (size == items.length) {
            items = Arrays.copyOf(items, size + (size >> 1));
            copies += size;
        }
        items[size++] = value;
    }

    int get(int index) {
        Objects.checkIndex(index, size);   // the array may be longer than size
        return items[index];
    }
}
```

A resize copies every element, which sounds expensive. Counting shows it is not. Copies happen when the size reaches each capacity $c_0, c_1, \dots, c_t$, and each capacity is about $\frac{2}{3}$ of the next:

$$
\text{total copies} = \sum_{j=0}^{t} c_j \le c_t \left(1 + \frac{2}{3} + \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^2 + \dots\right) = 3\,c_t \le 3n
$$

where:

- $c_j$ is the capacity at the $j$-th resize, so the $j$-th resize copies $c_j$ elements;
- $c_t$ is the last capacity that filled up, which is less than the number of elements added, $n$;
- the bracket is a geometric series with ratio $\frac{2}{3}$, whose sum is $\frac{1}{1 - 2/3} = 3$.

Example: adding $n = 50$ elements resizes at sizes 10, 15, 22, 33 and 49, copying $10 + 15 + 22 + 33 + 49 = 129$ elements, and $129 \le 3 \times 50 = 150$. The final capacity is 73. For $n = 1{,}000$ the lab counts 2,456 copies, within $3{,}000$. Adding the $n$ ordinary writes gives under $4n$ work in total, so each `add` is $O(1)$ **amortised**: averaged over the whole sequence, not promised for every single call.

Growing by a **fixed** amount fails this test. Adding 10 slots each time copies $10 + 20 + \dots + 990 = 10 \times \frac{99 \times 100}{2} = 49{,}500$ elements for 1,000 adds, twenty times more, and the gap grows like $n^2$. Doubling copies fewer elements than 1.5x (at most $2n$) but can leave half the array empty; 1.5x leaves at most a third empty. Java chose the smaller waste.

### Level 4: one pass instead of many shifts

Deleting several elements one at a time repeats the shifting. If the $k$ elements to delete all sit at the front of an array of $n$, the deletions shift $n - 1$, then $n - 2$, and so on:

$$
\text{shifts}_{\text{one by one}} = \sum_{j=1}^{k} (n - j) = kn - \frac{k(k+1)}{2}
$$

where:

- $n$ is the starting number of elements;
- $k$ is how many elements are deleted;
- $n - j$ is the cost of the $j$-th deletion at the front, when $n - j + 1$ elements remain.

Example: deleting the four zeros from `[0, 0, 0, 0, 5, 6, 7, 8]` one at a time costs $4 \times 8 - \frac{4 \times 5}{2} = 32 - 10 = 22$ shifts, which is $7 + 6 + 5 + 4$.

The cure is to keep two indices. `read` visits every element once; `write` marks where the next survivor goes. Each element is read once and written at most once, so the cost is $n$ reads, whatever $k$ is:

```java
static int removeZeros(int[] a) {
    int write = 0;
    for (int read = 0; read < a.length; read++) {
        if (a[read] != 0) a[write++] = a[read];
    }
    return write;                          // the new length: a[0..write) holds the survivors
}
```

On `[0, 1, 0, 3, 12]` this makes 5 reads and 3 writes and returns length 3, with `[1, 3, 12]` at the front. `ArrayList.removeIf` works the same way: it marks the victims first, then compacts the survivors in a single pass.

### Level 5: the array as its own lookup table

When the values are known to lie in $1..n$ and the array has $n$ slots, each value has a natural home:

$$
\operatorname{home}(v) = v - 1, \qquad 1 \le v \le n
$$

where:

- $v$ is a value stored in the array;
- $n$ is the array length;
- $\operatorname{home}(v)$ is the index that "belongs" to $v$.

Example: in an array of length 8, value 5 belongs at index 4 and value 1 at index 0. Value 9 or $-1$ has no home, because it lies outside $1..8$.

This turns the array into a set with $O(1)$ membership and **no extra memory**. To record "I have seen $v$", change something at index $v - 1$ that can be undone or read back later: flip its sign (Interview problem 1), or swap $v$ into that slot (Interview problem 3). A `HashSet` would do the same job with $O(n)$ extra space; the array's own indices are a hash table whose hash function is $v - 1$, with no collisions possible.

## Why it works and what it costs

**Address arithmetic is correct** because the block has no gaps and every element has the same size: element $i$ starts after exactly $i$ whole elements, which occupy $i \cdot s$ bytes.

**`insertAt` is correct.** The invariant of the loop is: *before the step for index `i`, the elements originally at `index..i-1` are untouched, and those originally at `i..size-1` now sit one place to the right.* Initially `i = size` and nothing has moved. Each step copies `a[i - 1]` into `a[i]`, a slot whose old value has already been moved on, so nothing is lost. When `i == index`, the whole tail has moved and `a[index]` is free for the new value.

**Compaction is correct.** The invariant is: *`a[0..write)` holds, in their original order, exactly the non-zero elements among `a[0..read)`.* Because `write <= read` at all times, writing into `a[write]` never destroys an element that has not been read yet.

**Costs**, with $n$ elements:

| Operation | Array (`int[]`) | `ArrayList` | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| read or write `a[i]` | $O(1)$ | $O(1)$ | one multiplication and one addition |
| append at the end | not possible | $O(1)$ amortised | at most $3n$ copies over $n$ appends |
| insert or delete at index $k$ | $O(n - k)$ | $O(n - k)$ | shift the tail; $n/2$ on average |
| search for a value | $O(n)$ | $O(n)$ | look at every element; $O(\log n)$ if sorted |
| delete $k$ elements matching a test | $O(n)$ with compaction | $O(n)$ with `removeIf` | each element read once |

Arrays also win on a cost the table hides: neighbours sit in the same cache line, so scanning an array is several times faster than following links of the same length.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Symptom | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Loop to `i <= a.length` | `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` on the last step | Valid indices are $0$ to $n - 1$: use `i < a.length` |
| Shift left to right when inserting | The same value is smeared over the whole tail | Insert right to left, delete left to right |
| Calling `list.remove(i)` inside a forward loop | The element right after each removed one is skipped, and the loop is $O(n^2)$ | `list.removeIf(...)`, or a read/write compaction |
| `list.remove(1)` on a `List<Integer>` | Removes the element at **index** 1, not the value 1 | `list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1))` |
| Adding to `Arrays.asList(...)` | `UnsupportedOperationException` | It is a fixed-size view of the array; copy it into `new ArrayList<>(...)` |
| `ArrayList<Integer>` for millions of numbers | Memory several times larger and slower scans, since each element is a separate object | Use `int[]`, or a primitive list class |
| Expecting `a == b` or `a.equals(b)` to compare contents | Two identical arrays are "not equal" | `Arrays.equals(a, b)` |

## Interview problems

Each solution starts with the mathematics. Once the formula is right, the code is short.

### 1. LeetCode 448: Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array (Easy)

**Problem.** An array of length $n$ holds values in $1..n$; some appear twice and others are missing. Return the missing ones, using no extra space apart from the answer. For `[4, 3, 2, 7, 8, 2, 3, 1]` the answer is `[5, 6]`.

**Math first.** Use Level 5: the sign of slot $v - 1$ records whether $v$ was seen.

$$
\text{missing} = \lbrace\, i + 1 : a_i > 0 \text{ after marking} \,\rbrace, \qquad \text{marking: } a_{\lvert v \rvert - 1} \leftarrow -\lvert a_{\lvert v \rvert - 1} \rvert \text{ for every } v
$$

where:

- $a_i$ is the value at index $i$;
- $\lvert v \rvert$ is the absolute value; it recovers the original value even after its own slot has been made negative;
- an index whose value is still positive was never anyone's home, so $i + 1$ never appeared.

Example: the values $4, 3, 2, 7, 8, 2, 3, 1$ mark indices $3, 2, 1, 6, 7, 1, 2, 0$. The array becomes `[-4, -3, -2, -7, 8, 2, -3, -1]`. Only indices 4 and 5 stay positive, so the missing values are $4 + 1 = 5$ and $5 + 1 = 6$.

**Idea.** One pass to mark, one pass to collect. Taking the absolute value before using a number as an index matters, because that number may already have been negated.

```java
static List<Integer> findDisappearedNumbers(int[] nums) {
    for (int v : nums) {
        int slot = Math.abs(v) - 1;        // value v is recorded at index v - 1
        if (nums[slot] > 0) nums[slot] = -nums[slot];
    }
    List<Integer> missing = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        if (nums[i] > 0) missing.add(i + 1);
    }
    return missing;
}
```

**Answer.** `[5, 6]` for the example, and `[2]` for `[1, 1]`. Two passes of $n$ steps, $2 \times 8 = 16$ steps here: $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra space.

### 2. LeetCode 238: Product of Array Except Self (Medium)

**Problem.** Return an array whose element $i$ is the product of every element except `nums[i]`, in $O(n)$ time and **without division**. For `[1, 2, 3, 4]` the answer is `[24, 12, 8, 6]`.

**Math first.** Split "everything except $i$" into the part on the left and the part on the right:

$$
\text{out}_i = L_i \cdot R_i, \qquad L_i = \prod_{j < i} a_j, \qquad R_i = \prod_{j > i} a_j
$$

where:

- $a_j$ is the input value at index $j$;
- $L_i$ is the product of everything left of $i$, with $L_0 = 1$ (an empty product);
- $R_i$ is the product of everything right of $i$, with $R_{n-1} = 1$.

Example: `[1, 2, 3, 4]`.

| $i$ | $L_i$ | $R_i$ | $\text{out}_i$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 1 | $2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 = 24$ | 24 |
| 1 | 1 | $3 \cdot 4 = 12$ | 12 |
| 2 | $1 \cdot 2 = 2$ | 4 | 8 |
| 3 | $1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 = 6$ | 1 | 6 |

**Idea.** A left-to-right pass writes $L_i$ into the answer; a right-to-left pass multiplies in $R_i$, kept in a single running variable. Division would fail on a zero and is forbidden anyway.

```java
static int[] productExceptSelf(int[] nums) {
    int n = nums.length;
    int[] answer = new int[n];
    int left = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {          // answer[i] = product of everything left of i
        answer[i] = left;
        left *= nums[i];
    }
    int right = 1;
    for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {     // times the product of everything right of i
        answer[i] *= right;
        right *= nums[i];
    }
    return answer;
}
```

**Answer.** `[24, 12, 8, 6]`; and `[-1, 1, 0, -3, 3]` gives `[0, 0, 9, 0, 0]`, since only index 2 avoids the zero: $(-1)(1)(-3)(3) = 9$. Two passes, $2n$ multiplications each: $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra space besides the output.

### 3. LeetCode 41: First Missing Positive (Hard)

**Problem.** Return the smallest positive integer not in an unsorted array, in $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra space. For `[3, 4, -1, 1]` the answer is 2.

**Math first.** An array of $n$ numbers can contain at most the $n$ values $1, 2, \dots, n$, so by the pigeonhole principle

$$
\text{answer} \in \lbrace 1, 2, \dots, n + 1 \rbrace, \qquad \text{answer} = \min \lbrace\, i + 1 : a_i \ne i + 1 \,\rbrace \text{ after every } v \in [1, n] \text{ is moved to index } v - 1
$$

where:

- $n$ is the array length;
- the answer is $n + 1$ only when all of $1..n$ are present;
- "moved to index $v - 1$" is Level 5's home, reached by swapping; values outside $[1, n]$ have no home and stay wherever the swaps leave them.

Example: $n = 4$, so the answer is one of $1, \dots, 5$. Placing `[3, 4, -1, 1]`:

- $i = 0$: 3 belongs at index 2. Swap: `[-1, 4, 3, 1]`. Now $-1$ has no home; move on.
- $i = 1$: 4 belongs at index 3. Swap: `[-1, 1, 3, 4]`. Now 1 belongs at index 0. Swap: `[1, -1, 3, 4]`. $-1$ has no home.
- $i = 2, 3$: 3 and 4 are already home.

That is 3 swaps. Scanning `[1, -1, 3, 4]`, index 1 holds $-1 \ne 2$, so the answer is **2**.

**Idea.** Every swap puts one value into its home permanently, so there are at most $n$ swaps in total, even though there is a `while` inside the `for`. The condition `nums[nums[i] - 1] != nums[i]` stops when the home already holds the same value, which prevents an endless loop on duplicates such as `[1, 1]`.

```java
static int firstMissingPositive(int[] nums) {
    placeValuesHome(nums);
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        if (nums[i] != i + 1) return i + 1;
    }
    return nums.length + 1;
}

static int placeValuesHome(int[] nums) {   // returns the number of swaps
    int swaps = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        while (nums[i] >= 1 && nums[i] <= nums.length && nums[nums[i] - 1] != nums[i]) {
            int home = nums[i] - 1;        // value v belongs at index v - 1
            int moved = nums[home];
            nums[home] = nums[i];
            nums[i] = moved;
            swaps++;
        }
    }
    return swaps;
}
```

**Answer.** 2 for `[3, 4, -1, 1]`; 3 for `[1, 2, 0]` (1 and 2 present, so $n + 1 = 3$); 1 for `[7, 8, 9, 11, 12]`; 2 for `[1, 1]`. At most $n$ swaps plus $n$ loop steps plus $n$ scan steps, so at most $3 \times 4 = 12$ steps for the example: $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra space.

## Mathematical Abstraction

An array is a function from indices to values, stored so that the function can be evaluated by arithmetic:

$$
A : \lbrace 0, 1, \dots, n - 1 \rbrace \to V, \qquad \operatorname{addr}(i) = b + i \cdot s, \qquad
\text{cost} =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{read or write } A(i) \\
n - k & \text{insert at index } k \\
\le 3 \text{ amortised} & \text{append with 1.5x growth}
\end{cases}
$$

where:

- $V$ is the set of values the array may hold, and $n$ is its length;
- $b$ is the base address and $s$ the size of one element in bytes;
- $k$ is the insertion index, and the cost counts element moves.

Example: for the six `int` scores at base $b = 1000$, reading index 3 is one sum, $1000 + 3 \times 4 = 1012$; inserting at index 2 moves $6 - 2 = 4$ scores; and 50 appends to an `ArrayList`-style array copy 129 elements in total, $129 / 50 \approx 2.6 \le 3$ per append. Fast reads, slow middle inserts and cheap amortised appends all follow from "one block, no gaps".
